query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Short-range ordering (SRO) in CoCrFeMnNi-based high-entropy alloys, modulated by small changes in Cr content, governs the retention or loss of toughness by altering the stacking-fault energy and dislocation/twin interactions. Moderate Cr doping promotes beneficial SRO that enhances strain hardening and toughness, whereas excessive SRO from higher Cr additions facilitates brittle pathways and reduces toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy in its single-phase FCC state, homogenized to minimize pre-existing second phases and residual segregation.
generation.intervention: Incrementally vary Cr content from 0 to 10 at.% relative to the baseline CoCrFeMnNi composition and perform fracture toughness measurements alongside in situ electron microscopy of deformation mechanisms.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing from cryogenic (≈77 K) up to 800 K, controlled strain rates, and air environment to compare fracture behavior across doping levels and temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range ordering that influences local stacking-fault energy, regulating dislocation slip/twinning activity and crack propagation paths.
generation.mechanism: Cr additions enhance local chemical order, reducing stacking-fault energy to encourage twin formation and dislocation interactions that raise strain hardening and fracture resistance. Excessive Cr promotes overly strong SRO or local embrittlement sites, thus reducing ductility and toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: At moderate doping (e.g., 3–7 at.% Cr), toughness and strain hardening increase relative to the undoped baseline, especially at lower temperatures, whereas high Cr additions ( > 10 at.%) lead to decreased toughness through partial embrittlement.
generation.baseline: A reference CoCrFeMnNi alloy without extra Cr additions, whose toughness is well characterized at ambient and cryogenic temperatures.
generation.boundary: Valid for FCC single-phase states without significant secondary phases. At doping levels or temperatures that induce substantial phase transformations, or at very high temperatures (> ~800 K), the proposed SRO-mediated mechanism may not govern toughness.
generation.uncertainty: Exact doping thresholds that maximize toughness are not fully established and may shift with processing history or minor compositional variations.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce multiple alloy variants with Cr doping increments (0, 3, 7, 10 at.%). Conduct standardized fracture toughness tests (e.g., J-integral or KIC) in conjunction with in situ TEM or SEM fractography at 77 K, RT, and 800 K.
measurements: Electron microscopy of dislocation structures, twins, and crack-tip regions
Quantification of short-range ordering via diffraction or atom probe tomography
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If systematic variation of Cr content does not correlate with changes in measured toughness or dislocation/twinning activity (i.e., if samples display no consistent relationship between SRO, SFE, and fracture toughness), the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) of the Cantor type (CoCrFeMnNi) are widely recognized as model systems for studying the relationships between composition, microstructure, and functional performance. In this study, atomized Cantor alloy powders were consolidated using spark plasma sintering (SPS) under systematically varied process parameters (temperature and dwell time). The densification behavior, microstructural evolution, and mechanical response were investigated using Archimedes’ density measurements, Vickers hardness testing, compression tests, scanning electron microscopy, and EDS mapping. The results reveal a non-linear relationship between sintering temperature and densification, with maximum relative densities obtained at 1050 °C and 1100 °C for short dwell times. Despite the ultrafast nature of SPS, grain growth was observed, particularly at elevated temperatures and extended dwell times, challenging the assumption that SPS inherently limits grain coarsening. All sintered samples retained a single-phase FCC structure with homogeneous elemental distribution, and no phase segregation or secondary precipitates were detected. AbstractDamage tolerance can be an elusive characteristic of structural materials requiring both high strength and ductility, properties that are often mutually exclusive. High-entropy alloys are of interest in this regard. Specifically, the single-phase CrMnFeCoNi alloy displays tensile strength levels of ∼1 GPa, excellent ductility (∼60–70%) and exceptional fracture toughness (KJIc>200 MPa√m). Here through the use of in situ straining in an aberration-corrected transmission electron microscope, we report on the salient atomistic to micro-scale mechanisms underlying the origin of these properties. We identify a synergy of multiple deformation mechanisms, rarely achieved in metallic alloys, which generates high strength, work hardening and ductility, including the easy motion of Shockley partials, their interactions to form stacking-fault parallelepipeds, and arrest at planar slip bands of undissociated dislocations. We further show that crack propagation is impeded by twinned, nanoscale bridges that form between the near-tip crack faces and delay fracture by shielding the crack tip. High-entropy and medium-entropy alloys are presumed to have a configurational entropy as high as that of an ideally mixed solid solution (SS) of multiple elements in near-equal proportions. However, enthalpic interactions inevitably render such chemically disordered SSs rare and metastable, except at very high temperatures. Here we highlight the wide variety of local chemical ordering (LCO) that sets these concentrated SSs apart from traditional solvent-solute ones. Using atomistic simulations, we reveal that the LCO of the multi-principal-element NiCoCr SS changes with alloy processing conditions, producing a wide range of generalized planar fault energies. We show that the LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities. This influences the selection of dislocation pathways in slip, faulting, and twinning, and increases the lattice friction to dislocation motion via a nanoscale segment detrapping mechanism. In summary, our results demonstrate that in the dual-phase Cantor-like high-entropy alloy, it is the continuous in situ phase transformation that provides the dominant contribution to strain hardening. As distinct from traditional dual-phase alloys, in the DP-HEAs the motivation for this transformation lies in the creation of stacking-fault networks, which seed the fcc → hcp transformation and which are intrinsically formed because of the fluctuation in lattice friction associated with concentration waves. However, it is worth noting that the fracture toughness of these TRIP HEAs may not be similarly enhanced compared to the Cantor alloy, particularly at decreasing temperatures. Despite the stress-induced TRIP effect of the fcc → hcp transformation, which acts to enhance the degree of strain hardening to the benefit of strength and ductility, fracture toughness is also a function of the inherent toughness of the product hcp phase, and this ε-martensite phase, despite its strength, tends to be quite brittle and not characterized by any significant degree of toughness. The exceptional mechanical strength of medium/high-entropy alloys has been attributed to hardening in random solid solutions. Here, we evidence non-random chemical mixing in a CrCoNi alloy, resulting from short-range ordering. A data-mining approach of electron nanodiffraction enabled the study, which is assisted by neutron scattering, atom probe tomography, and diffraction simulation using first-principles theory models. Two samples, one homogenized and one heat-treated, are observed. In both samples, results reveal two types of short-range-order inside nanoclusters that minimize the Cr–Cr nearest neighbors (L12) or segregate Cr on alternating close-packed planes (L11). The L11 is predominant in the homogenized sample, while the L12 formation is promoted by heat-treatment, with the latter being accompanied by a dramatic change in dislocation-slip behavior. These findings uncover short-range order and the resulted chemical heterogeneities behind the mechanical strength in CrCoNi, providing general opportunities for atomistic-structure study in concentrated alloys for the design of strong and ductile materials. chosen.lever: Adjust Cr content from 0 to ~10 at.% in CoCrFeMnNi base composition
chosen.technique: Fracture toughness experiments and in-situ TEM to assess dislocation/twinning interactions
chosen.conditions: Wide temperature range (77 K to 800 K) and multiple strain rates in air
chosen.why: Systematic doping to modulate microstructure and the associated mechanical response is a standard, direct approach in materials science to test mechanistic hypotheses of toughness retention or loss in high-entropy alloys. By comparing fracture and microstructural evolution across Cr doping levels and temperatures, the study can conclusively link short-range ordering and stacking-fault energy changes to toughness, validating or refuting the proposed mechanism.
